title: Episode 146: The Tragic Summer of 1881: The Assassination and 79-Day Agony of James A. Garfield

On the sweltering morning of July 2, 1881, President James A. Garfield walked into the Baltimore and Potomac train station in Washington, anticipating a joyful summer vacation and college reunion. Seconds later, two pistol shots shattered the waiting room. The shooter was Charles J. Guiteau, a delusional, mentally deranged attorney who believed God had commanded him to remove the President so that Vice President Chester A. Arthur would grant him a diplomatic consulship to Paris. Yet the bullet did not kill James A. Garfield. What followed was a seventy-nine-day medical nightmare of unwashed hands, unsterilized probes, and medical malpractice by doctors who rejected Joseph Lister's antiseptic surgery. Discover how Alexander Graham Bell invented the world's first metal detector to find the bullet, and how an agonizing summer transformed a shattered nation.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our portrait of James A. Garfield with one of the most poignant and tragic stories in American history. For seventy-nine days in the summer of 1881, the entire world watched in heartbreak as a beloved president fought for his life against infection and medical hubris in a sweltering White House bedroom. Here is George with the full story of Garfield's final, heroic battle.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: TWO SHOTS AT THE BALTIMORE AND POTOMAC STATION
Saturday, July 2, 1881, dawned humid and oppressively hot in the nation's capital. President James A. Garfield was in exuberant spirits. His beloved wife Crete was recovering from a dangerous bout of malaria in Elberon, New Jersey, and Garfield was on his way to join her for a long-delayed summer vacation, culminating in a reunion at his alma mater, Williams College. Arriving at the Baltimore and Potomac train station on Sixth Street around nine o'clock, Garfield walked through the ladies' waiting room arm-in-arm with Secretary of State James G. Blaine. There were no Secret Service bodyguards; presidents in the Gilded Age walked openly among the public.

Stepping out from behind a wooden bench, a scrawny, hollow-cheeked man dressed in a threadbare black suit raised a silver-plated .44-caliber British Bulldog revolver. The assassin was Charles Julius Guiteau, a thirty-nine-year-old drifter, failed lawyer, and religious eccentric who had stalked the President for weeks. Guiteau pulled the trigger twice. The first bullet grazed Garfield's arm, slicing through his coat. The second bullet tore into the President's lower back, shattering his eleventh rib and knocking him instantly to the marble floor. As police officers and furious bystanders tackled Guiteau to the ground, the deranged gunman shrieked: 'I did it! I am a Stalwart of the Stalwarts! Arthur is President now!' Garfield lay in a pool of blood, vomiting and gasping for breath, whispering faintly: 'My God, what is this?'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE MEDICAL HUBRIS OF DR. BLISS
Within minutes, the train station was in total bedlam. Bystanders carried the wounded President upstairs to a dusty second-floor office and laid him on a dirty horsehair mattress. A swarm of local physicians rushed to the scene. The first doctor inserted his unwashed finger directly into the bullet wound, searching for the projectile. Over the next hour, half a dozen different doctors poked unsterilized fingers, metal probes, and porcelain sounders into Garfield's back, tearing a false path through his muscle and introducing lethal bacteria into his body.

Taking control of the case was Dr. Doctor Willard Bliss—a prominent Washington surgeon whose actual first name was 'Doctor.' Bliss was an arrogant, autocratic physician who immediately barred all other doctors, including Garfield's trusted family physicians, from managing the patient. In 1881, the revolutionary work of British surgeon Joseph Lister regarding antiseptic technique and germ theory was widely accepted in Europe, but mainstream American medicine largely ridiculed it as European nonsense. Dr. Bliss scoffed at carbolic acid sprays, rarely washed his hands between patients, and repeatedly probed the wound with unsterilized instruments. Modern forensic pathologists universally agree that Garfield's wound was not fatal: the bullet had missed his spine, his aorta, and all vital organs, lodging harmlessly in the muscular wall of his abdomen. It was not Charles Guiteau's bullet that killed James A. Garfield; it was the filthy fingers and instruments of his attending physicians.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SWELTERING WHITE HOUSE AND THE NAVY'S AIR CONDITIONER
Garfield was transported back to the White House in an army wagon padded with mattresses. The temperature inside the second-floor presidential bedroom hovered between ninety and one hundred degrees, with stifling Washington humidity turning the mansion into an incubator for disease. Garfield suffered from excruciating back pain, relentless nausea, and recurring fevers. In an era before modern air conditioning, engineers and naval officers mobilized to find relief for the suffering commander-in-chief.

A brilliant naval engineer named Ralph Shuman designed an ingenious mechanical cooling apparatus—the world's first rudimentary air conditioner. The device consisted of a massive cast-iron box filled with six tons of ice, through which an electric fan blew air over cotton sheets soaked in ice water and charcoal. The cool, dehumidified air was pumped through large canvas air ducts into Garfield's bedroom, lowering the temperature by twenty degrees and providing the dying President with his only moments of physical comfort. Meanwhile, outside the White House gates, tens of thousands of citizens gathered in silence, weeping, praying, and waiting for the medical bulletins posted on the fences every two hours.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL AND THE INDUCTION BALANCE
Desperate to locate the bullet so Dr. Bliss could surgically extract it, the nation turned to its most famous inventor: thirty-four-year-old Alexander Graham Bell. Working feverishly in his Washington laboratory day and night, Bell invented an entirely new electromagnetic device called the 'induction balance'—the ancestor of the modern metal detector. The device used two balanced electromagnetic coils connected to a telephone receiver. If metal entered the magnetic field, it disrupted the balance, producing a distinct hum or clicking sound in the earpiece.

On July 26, Bell arrived at the White House and carried his apparatus into Garfield's darkened bedroom. As Bell gently moved the listening wand over the President's body, the earpiece began to hum faintly, but the signal was confusing and diffuse. Bell returned on August 1 with an improved version of the machine. Once again, the wand produced an irregular, widespread buzzing across the right side of the President's torso. What Bell did not realize—and what Dr. Bliss arrogantly failed to disclose—was that Garfield was lying on a patented steel coil spring mattress, an extraordinary luxury at the time. The metal springs beneath the bed had completely distorted Bell's magnetic field. Furthermore, Bliss insisted that the bullet was on the right side of the body, refusing to allow Bell to test the left side, where the bullet actually lay buried safely away from danger.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT WASTING AND THE JOURNEY TO THE SEA
By August, systemic blood poisoning—sepsis—had taken complete hold of the President's body. Massive, purulent abscesses erupted across his chest and hips; his digestive system collapsed, and his weight plummeted from two hundred and ten muscular pounds to less than one hundred and thirty pounds. The athletic, vibrant canal boy was reduced to a hollow, jaundiced skeleton. Yet through seventy days of agonizing torture, Garfield never complained. He smiled faintly at his wife Crete, joked gently with his nurses, and patiently bore every painful probing of his infected wound.

Recognizing that the President was dying, Crete pleaded with Dr. Bliss to take him away from the stifling swamp air of Washington to the sea breeze of Elberon, New Jersey. On September 6, a special train fitted with cushioned stretchers carried Garfield north. To bring the train directly to the cottage without jolting the President, two thousand local citizens and workers worked through the night to build a spur track of railroad lines running three thousand feet directly to the cottage door. When the engine's steam pressure was shut down to avoid frightening Garfield, hundreds of local townspeople quietly took hold of the passenger cars and pushed the train by hand across the sand dunes right up to the porch.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE FINAL BREATH AT ELBERON
For a few brief days in the ocean cottage at Elberon, Garfield seemed to rally. Propped up in bed by open windows, he stared out at the vast blue Atlantic Ocean, watching the white sails of passing ships and breathing in the cool salt air. He asked for pen and paper and scribbled a single Latin word: 'Spes'—hope. But the infection was unstoppable. On September 17, severe chills and violent chest spasms racked his body. Pneumonia and blood clots invaded his lungs.

On the evening of September 19, 1881—the eighteenth anniversary of his heroism at the Battle of Chickamauga—Garfield awoke from a deep sleep around ten o'clock, clutching his chest in agony. 'Oh, Swaim, there is a pain here,' he whispered to his chief of staff, General David Swaim. 'This pain, this terrible pain!' Minutes later, James A. Garfield closed his eyes for the last time. He was forty-nine years old, having served as president for exactly two hundred days—eighty of them spent in agonizing pain. Church bells tolled across every city in America; in London, Queen Victoria ordered court mourning, and for the first time in British history, flags across the British Empire flew at half-mast for an American president.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE RECKONING AND THE TRANSFORMATION OF AMERICAN POLITICS
Charles Guiteau was put on trial for murder in the fall of 1881 in one of the most sensational media spectacles of the century. Guiteau treated the courtroom as his personal theater, singing hymns, insulting the judge, and arguing that God had ordered the killing. Crucially, Guiteau made a defense that history would later confirm: 'I concede that the President died of malpractice. The doctors killed Garfield, I only shot him.' The jury took just one hour to convict him of murder, and Guiteau was hanged in June 1882. An autopsy performed on Garfield revealed that the bullet was completely encysted in benign scar tissue, precisely where it could have stayed for the rest of his life without causing harm. He had died entirely of septicemia caused by unwashed medical care.

Yet Garfield's agonizing martyrdom profoundly changed the United States. The horrific spectacle of a president murdered by a deranged office-seeker finally broke the back of the corrupt spoils system. Shocked by the tragedy, the nation demanded real civil service reform. And in an astonishing transformation that no one could have anticipated, the man who succeeded him—Chester A. Arthur, the very symbol of the machine politics that had spawned Guiteau—renounced his old cronies, broke with Roscoe Conkling, and signed the historic Pendleton Civil Service Act into law. In death, James A. Garfield achieved the reform he had fought for his entire life.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The tragic death of James A. Garfield reminded the American people of the fragile human cost of political corruption. His suffering united a divided nation and compelled an indifferent political system to finally embrace merit and integrity. Next week, we conclude our Gilded Age trilogy with Chester A. Arthur—the dapper New York dandy and machine boss whose noble transformation in the White House astonished his enemies and redeemed his soul. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
